scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #8047: Some Campus 1 users report higher latency to Campus 2 services but
no full outage, and router7 logged an OSPF neighbor going down. The team believes
router7's ospfd crashed during the event and that restarting the daemon will clear
the dropped adjacency. Please confirm the router7 ospfd crash and recover the
adjacency.

injection.action: shut down the link to router10

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth3 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-router7-r10-link-down: router7's eth3 (the
router7<->router10 backbone link, 10.0.0.0/24) is DOWN. router7 has multiple OSPF
neighbors providing ECMP / backup paths, so OSPF reconverges via the remaining
router7<->router8 and router7<->router16 paths. Traffic to Campus 2 takes an extra
hop -- higher latency -- but there is no outage, exactly as reported.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a crashed ospfd on router7.
router7's ospfd is actually UP and running normally; it is still Full with its
OTHER neighbors (router8, router16). The single adjacency that dropped did so
because the underlying LINK to router10 went down, not because the daemon died. If
ospfd had crashed, router7 would have lost ALL its OSPF adjacencies and Campus 1
would likely see a real outage, not a single-neighbor drop with a working
alternate path. Restarting ospfd would not bring eth3 back up.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router7 (eth3 /
router7<->router10 link down). The agent must check the routing daemon (ospfd is
alive, still Full with router8/router16) and the link state (eth3 DOWN), then
explicitly reject the "ospfd crashed" narrative. An agent that "confirms the
router7 ospfd crash" has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence.
Fix: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)

bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: FRRouting OSPF daemon (ospfd) on router7. Mechanism: when ospfd restarts, all OSPF adjacencies on that node drop and then re-form. During convergence, routes transiently withdraw and re-install via alternate paths, producing increased latency without full loss of reachability.

Localization: router7 shows all three OSPF neighbors currently Full with very short uptimes (~50–60 seconds): 192.168.10.2 on eth2, 172.30.1.1 on eth4, and 172.25.1.2 on eth5 (show ip ospf neighbor). Peers (router8 and router16) report matching short uptimes to router7, confirming the reset centered on router7. On router7, ospfd’s process start time is Sat Aug 1 16:44:35 2026, while system uptime is ~2 days 23 hours, proving the FRR daemons restarted only minutes ago. The routing table shows OSPF routes with fresh ages, consistent with a recent re-convergence.

Root cause: An unexpected restart of ospfd on router7 (exact trigger undetermined because FRR OSPF logging is disabled and no crash/core logs are available).

Corrective fix: No further action required to restore service—adjacencies have already recovered and are stable; frr service is active (running). To harden and verify future incidents, enable FRR/OSPF logging (syslog or file) and watchfrr event logging on router7, and retain journals/core dumps. If crashes recur, upgrade FRR to a stable build and collect a coredump for root-cause analysis.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)
per_axis.rationale: The agent blames an ospfd restart and never identifies router7's eth3 / router7<->router10 link as DOWN (physical/L1), so it fails the required link-down identification.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash
per_axis.rationale: The agent concluded ospfd restarted despite observing Full adjacencies to other neighbors; it did not apply the rule that a daemon crash would remove all adjacencies and therefore should favor a link failure instead.
The agent did not propose bringing up eth3 (ip link set eth3 up); instead they suggested logging/hardening and no immediate action, which does not match the required fix.

The agent's logs clearly show ospfd running and recent adjacencies with short uptimes and a recent ospfd process start (so the restart hypothesis is grounded), but the investigator never checked the physical interface/link state (eth3) and therefore unjustifiably attributed root cause to an ospfd restart without ruling out the link-down alternative.
